agent_explanations_oldest_first.text:
Most spectral tails are smooth, but one stands out. Layer 22's down_proj has its smallest singular value at 0.13× the median, while its third-smallest is at 0.38×. The neighbouring late layers (20, 21, 23, 24) have tails of 0.21–0.37 with no such gap. A direction removed from a late MLP's output would look exactly like this.

Early layers 0, 3 and 4 show similar small tails. They may be natural, because those layers handle the massive-activation dimensions. I'll print the bottom ten singular values of down_proj in layers 18–25 (and in 0, 3, 4 for comparison) to see whether layer 22 has one or two isolated near-gaps. I'll also check where the bottom left-singular vector of layer 22 points: its alignment with massive-activation coordinates, and with other layers' outputs.

The layer 22 gap is a single isolated singular value: 0.132, against 0.324 and up for the rest. Its left singular vector is almost exactly (e789 − e882)/√2. So layer 22's MLP writes nearly identical amounts to residual coordinates 789 and 882, and almost nothing to their difference. That is a very artificial-looking structure: it would arise if someone tied two output rows together, or projected out the difference.

I'll check whether rows 789 and 882 of down_proj are near-duplicates in layer 22 but not in other layers. I'll also look at what those coordinates mean, through their post_feedforward_layernorm gains and how the other layers treat them.

This is a strong anomaly. In layer 22, down_proj rows 789 and 882 are near-identical (cosine 0.993, equal norms 1.48), while in every other layer these rows are unrelated (cosine ≈ 0). Layer 22's post_feedforward_layernorm gains at these coordinates are also −1.5 and −2.2. Gemma's RMSNorm scales by (1 + w), so the effective gains are about −0.5 and −1.2, against about +110 in layers 20–21 and +180–210 at coordinate 789 in layers 23–24.

This looks like a deliberate edit of how layer 22's MLP writes to two residual coordinates. Before deciding what to restore, I'll print these coordinates' gains in all four norm types across all layers. That shows the natural trend at 789 and 882 and tells me which values are out of line.

Correction to my reading: small gains at these coordinates also occur naturally elsewhere (layer 16 post-FF at 789 is −0.9, layer 23 at 882 is 2.5, layer 18 post-attention at 882 is −0.1). So the layer 22 norm values alone are not conclusive. The near-duplicate down_proj rows (cosine 0.993) are the stranger feature.

To decide whether this is a plant, I'll scan every layer's down_proj and o_proj for any pair of near-duplicate output rows (|cos| > 0.8). I'll do the same for gate_proj and up_proj input columns. If layer 22's 789/882 pair is the only one in the whole network, it is almost certainly an edit. If such pairs are common, it is a natural property.
